a diferencia de buena parte de la banca: unlike much of the regional free banking, Banco de Barranquilla had institutional continuity: its successor, Banco Comercial de Barranquilla, survived until the 1960s, long after most of its contemporaries had disappeared.
a diferencia de la casi totalidad de los: unlike nearly all Antioquian banking establishments, which were concentrated in Medellín, Banco de Oriente operated from Rionegro —the former seat of the 1863 Convention and a commercial center that, thanks to the mining boom in the Santa Rosa and Rionegro highlands, had supplied the mines of northern and eastern Antioquia since the eighteenth century.
A diferencia de la pieza transicional de: Unlike the transitional 1791 2-escudo piece in the collection, this 1-escudo coin already bears the official, definitive portrait design of
a diferencia de la serie regular de circ: unlike the regular paper series of the New Taiwan Dollar, this commemorative banknote was produced entirely in polymer, becoming the only plastic copy ever issued by Taiwan.
a diferencia de las casas comerciales fa: unlike the family commercial houses that also issued their own banknotes, the Bank of Medellín was constituted as a banking company properly speaking. Studies on banking penetration in Antioquia place Banco de Antioquia and Banco de Medellín among the entities with the largest number of customers in the region, in contrast to more family-oriented houses with limited reach such as Vicente B. Villa é Hijos.
a diferencia de las demás denominaciones: unlike Hong Kong’s other denominations, issued by three authorized commercial banks, the $10 note is issued directly by the Hong Kong SAR Government through the HKMA. It was reintroduced in 2002 in response to public demand to retain the denomination as a banknote rather than only as a coin.
A diferencia de las emisiones de &ldquo;: Unlike the “hybrid bust” issues of later eras, this piece bears the official and authentic portrait of
a diferencia de las generaciones posteri: unlike later generations of the substrate, this first version became brittle and was prone to tearing completely from a small notch on the edge, prompting Banco Central do Brasil to remove it from active circulation.
a diferencia de las libranzas bancarias: unlike private bank drafts, this 1961 voucher was issued directly by the administration of the Department of Antioquia, with the signatures of the Secretary of Finance, the Undersecretary and the General Administrator of the Treasury.
A diferencia de las series anteriores, c: Unlike earlier series, which focused almost exclusively on national heroes and statesmen, the mid-1990s Ten Thousand Pesos banknotes reflect a more plural Colombia: the 1994 note commemorates Indigenous communities with a portrait of an Emberá woman and a colorful collage of birds and national biodiversity; the 1995 note returns to Policarpa Salavarrieta, “La Pola”, an independence martyr, with a rural scene on the reverse. Both bear the red overprint “SAMPLE WITHOUT VALUE” and zero serial numbers.
A diferencia de los actuales billetes de: Unlike current Federal Reserve notes (green seal), these 1929 banknotes were direct obligations of the issuing regional bank, not of the Federal Reserve System as a whole, and circulated relatively briefly, mainly in the early 1930s.
a diferencia de los billetes de bancos c: unlike banknotes from capital-city banks printed by foreign firms, this specimen came from D. Paredes’s local lithographic shop in Bogotá, using limestone plates to transfer the design to paper —a common practice among smaller regional banks; indeed, this bank’s notes were known for lacking a printer’s imprint.
A diferencia de los billetes de bancos p: Unlike the private bank notes of the free banking era, this copy is a state public debt note — issued directly by the Treasury of a sovereign state of the federation, and not by a bank entity—, which is more akin to the 1861 note of the United States Treasury of New Granada than to the role of the Colombian commercial banks of the last third of the nineteenth century.
a diferencia de los billetes de circulac: unlike circulating banknotes from the free-banking era, this piece is a mortgage certificate —a debt security backed by real-estate mortgages and authorized to circulate with fiduciary force under a specific legal framework: Law 24 of 1905 and the contract signed by the National Government and El Banco de Colombia on February 6, 1912.
a diferencia de los billetes íntegrament: unlike the fully plastic banknotes of the Guardian® technology (used by Brunei or Australia), this Qatari banknote retains a traditional base made of high-security cotton paper, in which De La Rue integrates a polymer Optiks® band as an additional security element, not as a complete substrate.
a diferencia de los fraccionarios, prese: unlike the fractional denominations, it features a joint (jugate) portrait of the five Ringling brothers in an oval at left, the denomination “ONE DOLLAR” in a central cartouche, lions in the upper corners, and elephants in the lower corners, with a blue Series A letter. Signed by P. L. Gust and O. L. Gust.
a diferencia de muchos billetes de polím: unlike many polymer banknotes worldwide, this denomination omits portraits and relies entirely on the bauhinia flower — Hong Kong’s floral symbol — and geometric patterns as its central motif.
a diferencia de otras denominaciones, el: unlike other denominations, the obverse features a composite portrait of four ordinary Nigerian citizens representing the country’s ethnic and cultural diversity, with a triangular tactile mark in the upper-left corner.
a diferencia de otros bancos bogotanos d: Unlike other Bogota banks of the time, Banco de la Unión operated under the corporate name of its founders, “Palau, Corrales & Compañía”, a common model among the banking and commercial houses of Bogotá in 1883, where private credit and import trade used to go hand in hand.
a diferencia de un billete bancario ordi: unlike an ordinary bank note, this voucher documents a “floating debt” — the result of the conversion of documents that represented liquid credits and recognized against the State by the Executive Branch, converted into a short-term negotiable instrument.
a diferencia del billete de Un Peso &mda: unlike the One Peso banknote —restamped under Decree N.° 517—, this Ten Pesos specimen carries a different formula: “This banknote is treated in every respect as those of the Banco Nacional and circulates under the guarantee of the Republic. Decree N.° 509 of October 30, 1899”. Both decrees, promulgated on the same day, show that the government issued specific provisions —possibly by bank or denomination— to formalize the reuse of private banknotes as circulating money during the fiscal emergency of the Thousand Days’ War.
a diferencia del recibo de contribución: unlike the receipt of voluntary contribution from this same collection, this document is one of the debt notes that the Junta issued directly on behalf of the Republic of Cuba in Arms, following the loan of twenty million pesos authorized on June 1, 1869 to finance the Liberation Army during the Ten Years' War.
A finales del siglo XIX, mientras la ban: In the late nineteenth century, as free banking transformed Colombia's financial landscape with dozens of regional issuers, some of those same private capitals sought opportunities outside the country. Central America, with its own economies in formation and scarce local banking infrastructure, was a natural destination for Colombian investors with experience in the issuance and management of paper money.

Reunir el Cien Pesos Oro de distintos añ: Collecting the Cien Pesos Oro from different issue years makes it possible to trace, through a single banknote type, the evolution of signatures, printers, and security varieties in Colombian paper money during the second half of the 20th century —an approachable form of collecting that also reveals the institutional history of Banco de la República.
Reunir el Diez Pesos Oro de distintos añ: Collecting the Diez Pesos Oro from different years makes it possible to trace, within a single series, the transition from the early postwar issue printed by American Bank Note Company to the Thomas De La Rue design that circulated for nearly a decade —a chapter of Colombian monetary history especially accessible to collectors.
Reunir el mismo billete de distintos dis: Collecting the same note from different Federal Reserve districts is one of the most accessible forms of thematic collecting: it tangibly illustrates the decentralized structure of the U.S. central banking system without requiring the pursuit of rarities or high-value varieties.

Ringling Bros. Circus se fundó en Barabo: Ringling Bros. Circus was founded in Baraboo in 1883, when the five Ringling brothers presented their first traveling show in the city. Fifty years later, during the Great Depression, the circus —merged with Barnum & Bailey since 1919— returned to its hometown for a special anniversary performance. The Chamber of Commerce used the occasion to issue this scrip, injecting about $50,000 into local circulation and leaving behind one of the sets of circus exonumia most coveted by collectors of “Greatest Show on Earth” memorabilia.

se autorizó una impresión limitada de bi: a limited printing of small-denomination notes (including 1 Real and 2 Reales) was authorized. Because the local population was deeply skeptical of paper and accustomed exclusively to precious metals, this money met enormous public resistance and low acceptance.
Se emitían bajo autoridad del Departamen: They were issued under the authority of the Department of Defense (not the Treasury), so they lack a Treasury seal. The Bureau of Engraving and Printing (BEP) produced them for the DoD; early series were also printed by Boston contractors Tudor Press and Forbes Lithograph.
se estima que se imprimieron cerca de ci: an estimated five million of these notes were printed, far exceeding the amount of silver actually collected. The surplus was acquired by Leopoldo Cerecedo Millán's commercial firm, which distributed them with commemorative overprints in 1920 —the reason unoverprinted examples such as this one are more coveted by collectors.
Se retiró a Monticello, donde proyectó l: He retired to Monticello, where he designed the University of Virginia. He died on July 4, 1826, the same day as John Adams and the fiftieth anniversary of the Declaration.
Se retiró a Villa de Leyva, donde murió: He retired to Villa de Leyva, where he died in 1823, already recognized during his lifetime as one of the ideological fathers of Spanish American independence.
Se retiró voluntariamente del poder en 1: He voluntarily relinquished power in 1797, an exceptional gesture at the time that strengthened the young nation's republican character in contrast to European monarchical models.

Según el Food and Nutrition Service, hac: According to the Food and Nutrition Service, by July 2004 all 50 states, the District of Columbia, the Virgin Islands, and Guam were operating statewide EBT systems (or territorial equivalents) to issue benefits. The paper coupons in this collection therefore come from the final phase of a distribution system that disappeared completely during that transition.
según el historiador Fernando Barriga de: according to historian Fernando Barriga del Diestro, El Banco de Panamá opened on August 14, 1869, amid a difficult period for the isthmus's economy: the opening of the transcontinental railroad in Utah diminished the importance of the Panama route, several foreign companies left the country, and the government had to seek loans from the bank itself during the crisis. A fire affecting the offices and business premises of Planas y Cía., together with partner Kelly's withdrawal, compounded these problems —factors that led to the bank's liquidation, leaving Panama without a single bank by about 1875.

You can begin collecting paper money with what you already carry in your wallet and grow your collection at your own pace. These are the keys to getting off to a good start.

Collectors enjoy the hobby more when they choose a unifying theme: a **country** (for example, Colombia), a **historical period**, a **theme** (portraits, wildlife, trains), an **issuing bank**, or a specific type such as **polymer** banknotes. A clear focus gives the collection coherence and makes purchasing decisions easier.

Later, many collectors turn to **numismatic fairs**, **auction houses**, and **specialized dealers**. Always buy from trusted sources and, for expensive pieces, prioritize those with authentication or clear provenance.

Broadly speaking, they are graded on a scale ranging from *Uncirculated* (UNC) to *Fair*, with *About Uncirculated*, *Very Fine*, and *Fine* in between. Folds, stains, tears, and worn corners reduce value. When starting out, learn to inspect these details before buying.
El papel moneda es frágil. Manipula los: Paper money is fragile. Handle banknotes with clean, dry hands—or with gloves—hold them by the edges, and store them in **sleeves made from acid-free material** (without PVC). Avoid direct sunlight, moisture, and heat. Never glue, mark, or "restore" them with tape: doing so destroys their value.

\"Numismática\" y \"notafilia\" suelen u: "Numismatics" and "notaphily" are often used as synonyms, but they refer to distinct disciplines within collecting. Understanding the difference helps you better define a collection, choose the appropriate catalogs, and preserve each piece as it deserves.
La numismática es la disciplina que estu: Numismatics is the discipline that studies and collects coins, medals, and, in its broadest sense, any object that has served as a means of payment throughout history. The term comes from the Greek *nómisma* ("coin"). It goes far beyond accumulating pieces: it encompasses the historical, artistic, and technical analysis of each coinage—the metals used, the mints, assayers, dies, and the economic context in which it circulated. A coin tells the story of the authority that issued it, the trade that moved it, and the society that used it.
La notafilia es la rama especializada qu: Notaphily is the specialized branch focused on the study and collection of banknotes and paper money. Its name combines the Latin *nota* ("banknote") with the Greek *philía* ("fondness"). A notaphilist is interested in the history of each issue, its design and engraving, watermarks and security features, authorized signatures, serial numbers, and the differences between issues from public and private banks. Paper money, more fragile and ephemeral than metal, also presents its own identification and conservation challenges.
La forma más sencilla de verlo: la notaf: The simplest way to see it is that notaphily is one branch of the large tree of numismatics. Numismatics is the broad umbrella—everything related to money as an object of study—and notaphily is its specialization in paper money. Therefore, in the broad sense, a banknote collector is also a numismatist, although they may prefer the more precise term.

Hay una escena que se repite en el mundo: There is a scene that repeats itself in the collecting world, and it is painful to witness. Someone inherits their father’s or grandfather’s banknote collection, lovingly stored in an album with plastic sleeves bought thirty years ago. They open the album and find the banknotes yellowed, their inks bleeding, stuck to the sleeve like old decals. When they try to peel one away, the surface of the paper remains attached to the plastic. Decades of history, patience, and investment ruined not by neglect, but precisely by the attempt to protect them.
El culpable tiene nombre: **PVC**, el cl: The culprit has a name: **PVC**, polyvinyl chloride, the most common and cheapest plastic on the market. And the solution also has a name: **Mylar**, an archival-quality polyester that museums, national libraries, and professional grading services have used for more than half a century. Without unnecessary jargon, but without avoiding the chemistry when it matters, this article explains why the difference between these two materials can mean the difference between a collection that survives for generations and one that silently destroys itself inside a drawer.
## El papel es materia viva (y frágil): ## Paper is a living (and fragile) material
Para entender por qué importa tanto el m: To understand why sleeve material matters so much, it helps to remember what a banknote is. Traditional paper money is made from cotton fibers—sometimes blended with linen—that are pressed and interwoven. It is an organic, hygroscopic material (it absorbs and releases moisture from the environment) and is chemically sensitive. The intaglio inks that give it texture, optically variable inks, metallic security threads, and watermarks all coexist in an object designed to last a few years in circulation, not decades in a display case.
Un billete sin circular, con su papel cr: An uncirculated banknote, with its crisp paper and intact relief, also retains something almost intangible: the paper’s **original sizing**, the stiffness and sheen that collectors and grading companies value so highly. All of it—fibers, inks, sizing—reacts with its surroundings: with light, moisture, airborne acids, and, above all, the materials that touch it directly for years. The sleeve is not a neutral accessory: it is the banknote’s immediate chemical environment, twenty-four hours a day, for decades.
Y aquí está la trampa: a simple vista, t: And here is the catch: at first glance, all transparent sleeves look the same. A newly purchased PVC sleeve looks clean, glossy, flexible, perfect. The damage it causes is not noticeable on the first day or even in the first year. It is a slow, cumulative, and—importantly—**irreversible** process.
## Qué es exactamente el PVC y por qué d: ## What exactly is PVC, and why does it destroy banknotes?
El cloruro de polivinilo es, en su estad: In its pure state, polyvinyl chloride is a rigid, brittle plastic. To turn it into the soft, flexible sleeves that bend without breaking, manufacturers add **plasticizers**: chemical compounds—usually phthalates—that can account for up to one-third of the material’s weight. That is the first problem, and it is enormous: the plasticizers are not chemically bonded to the plastic. Over time, they migrate. They leave the PVC and settle on whatever is in contact with it.
Sobre un billete, esa migración se manif: On a banknote, that migration appears as a greasy film, sometimes visible as an oily sheen on the paper. This film softens the inks, partially dissolves the pigments, and causes the banknote to adhere to the sleeve. When the collector finally notices something unusual and tries to remove the piece, the ink—or even the paper’s surface layer—remains stuck to the plastic. Veteran collectors speak of banknotes **«burned by PVC»**, and the expression is accurate: the damage resembles a chemical burn.
El segundo problema es todavía más insid: The second problem is even more insidious. PVC is chemically unstable: with heat, light, and the mere passage of time, the polymer degrades and releases **hydrochloric acid** as a gas. Yes, the same acid found in laboratories, in minute but constant concentrations, trapped inside a closed sleeve alongside the banknote. This acid attacks the paper’s cellulose fibers, which first turn yellow, then brown, and finally become brittle. It also attacks inks and corrodes metallic elements such as security threads and metallic inks.
Hay una tercera vía de daño que casi nad: There is a third path of damage that almost no one mentions: the effect accelerates itself. PVC degradation is **autocatalytic**, meaning that the acid it releases speeds up the decomposition of the plastic itself, which in turn releases more acid. That is why a collection can go ten years without visible symptoms and deteriorate dramatically over the next five. By the time the damage becomes evident, the process has already been advancing for years, and there is no turning back: no conservator can restore the paper’s lost sizing or replace dissolved ink.
Para quienes coleccionamos en el trópico: For those of us who collect in the tropics, there is an aggravating factor. Heat and humidity—the normal climate of Colombia’s hot regions, from Barranquilla to Villavicencio by way of Montería and Cali—multiply the speed of all these reactions. A PVC sleeve that might take twenty years to cause visible damage on the Bogotá savanna can do so in five on the coast. The enemy works fastest precisely where most of us collectors live.
## Cómo reconocer el PVC antes de que se: ## How to recognize PVC before it is too late
Lo más frustrante del asunto es que las: The most frustrating aspect is that PVC sleeves are rarely sold with labels identifying them as such. They are offered as «protective sleeves», «banknote sleeves», or a «paper money album», with no further information. Here are some practical clues for identifying them:
- **El olor.** El PVC plastificado tiene: - **The smell.** Plasticized PVC has a characteristic sweetish, «new plastic» smell, similar to a cheap shower curtain or the interior of a car fresh from the dealership. That smell is literally the plasticizer evaporating. Mylar and polypropylene have no smell. - **Excessive flexibility.** PVC sleeves are soft and rubbery, bend and wrinkle easily, and spring back into shape. Polyester is stiffer, with a «crisp» feel and a crease that leaves a mark. - **Price and origin.** Inexpensive albums with built-in pockets, especially old ones and generic unbranded products, should be considered suspect by default. If the seller cannot say what material the sleeve is made of, assume the worst. - **Signs in old sleeves.** Yellowing of the plastic itself, a sticky surface, stiffness where there used to be flexibility (a sign that the plasticizer has already migrated), or an oily film inside: all indicate PVC in active degradation. If an album shows any of these signs, the banknotes need to come out immediately, not next week.
Vale la pena decirlo con claridad: si un: It is worth stating clearly: if part of your collection is in sleeves whose material you do not know, the cost of replacing them with archival sleeves is a tiny fraction of the value of almost any collectible banknote. It is probably the best money you can spend in the entire hobby.
## Qué es el Mylar y por qué es diferent: ## What is Mylar, and why is it different?
«Mylar» es una marca registrada —origina: «Mylar» is a registered trademark—originally owned by DuPont and now by the Mylar Specialty Films group—for biaxially oriented polyethylene terephthalate film, a polyester known by its English abbreviation: **BoPET**. In the conservation world, archival-quality Mylar usually refers to specific varieties such as **Melinex 516**, the film used by the Library of Congress in the United States, national archives around the world, and the leading banknote grading services to encapsulate pieces.
La diferencia con el PVC no es de grado,: The difference from PVC is not one of degree, but of nature:
- **No contiene plastificantes.** El pol: - **It contains no plasticizers.** Polyester is flexible because of its own molecular structure, without additives that can migrate. There is no greasy film, no softened ink, and no banknotes stuck to the sleeve. What is not in the material cannot come out of it. - **It is chemically inert.** Under normal storage conditions, BoPET does not react with cellulose, inks, or metals. It releases no acids or gases. Chemically speaking, a banknote stored in Mylar is surrounded by nothing: the ideal scenario for a paper object. - **It remains stable over time.** While PVC degrades and accelerates its own decomposition, archival polyester retains its properties for decades. It easily passes the accelerated-aging tests required by conservation standards—such as the Photographic Activity Test (PAT) and ISO specifications for storage materials. - **It is a real barrier.** In addition to causing no damage itself, polyester provides good resistance to moisture and airborne pollutants, while its transparency and rigidity physically protect the banknote against accidental folds, oils from fingers, and abrasion.
Hay un matiz honesto que conviene añadir: An honest qualification should be added: Mylar is not magic. It is an inert material, not an active one. It does not neutralize acids already present in a banknote or correct prior damage. A banknote that spent years in PVC and is already contaminated will still have that residue on the paper even after you change the sleeve (in such cases, an assessment by a professional conservator is the only sensible course; never try to «clean» a banknote yourself). What Mylar guarantees is that, from the day the banknote enters the sleeve, its storage material ceases to be a threat.
## ¿Y los otros plásticos? El mapa compl: ## What about other plastics? The complete picture
Entre el villano (PVC) y el estándar de: Between the villain (PVC) and the gold standard (archival polyester) lies a middle ground that causes confusion. A quick overview:
- **Polipropileno y polietileno.** Ambos: - **Polypropylene and polyethylene.** Both are chemically stable and contain no plasticizers, so they are considered safe for contact with paper. They are used in affordable sleeves of acceptable quality. Their disadvantages compared with polyester are physical, not chemical: they are softer, scratch easily, provide less protection against handling, and are less transparent. For low-value banknotes or duplicates intended for trading, an additive-free polypropylene sleeve is a reasonable option. For the collection’s important pieces, polyester remains the answer. - **«Acetate».** Some older products use cellulose acetate, which over time develops what is known as «vinegar syndrome»: it degrades, releasing acetic acid (hence the vinegar smell), and damages whatever it holds. It should be avoided just like PVC. - **Glassine paper.** Translucent glassine envelopes, traditional in philately, are not plastic, but they deserve mention: ordinary glassine is slightly acidic and is not intended for decades of contact. If used, it should serve as temporary wrapping, never as permanent storage. - **Enemies that are not sleeves.** The list of preventable damage does not end with plastic: rubber bands (vulcanized rubber releases sulfur and leaves permanent dark marks), metal clips (rust), adhesive tape of any kind (a banknote’s single worst enemy after PVC), heat lamination (total and irreversible destruction of collectible value), and «magnetic» albums with self-adhesive pages. None of these things should be within a meter of a collection.
## En buena compañía: documentos famosos: ## In good company: famous documents that live in polyester
Si el argumento químico suena teórico, e: If the chemical argument sounds theoretical, the institutional argument is compelling: the most valuable paper objects on the planet are stored in exactly the material this article recommends.
La Biblioteca del Congreso de Estados Un: The Library of Congress in the United States pioneered polyester film encapsulation in the seventies, and today routinely applies it to its collection of historical maps, nineteenth-century newspapers, and manuscripts: the document is sealed between two sheets of inert polyester, allowing it to be consulted without ever being touched. The country’s National Archives use the same technique for thousands of frequently consulted documents. And for their absolute treasures—the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution—they took the principle to its extreme: sealed chambers filled with argon gas, without a single reactive molecule around the paper. It is the museum version of the same idea that a Mylar sleeve applies in your home: surrounding the document with nothing.
La Biblioteca Británica protege manuscri: The British Library protects manuscripts and historical documents with Melinex, the same archival-quality polyester film mentioned earlier. And there is no need to look that far away: in Colombia, the **Archivo de Bogotá** manufactures its own conservation units—polyester envelopes and rolls, folders, and boxes made with «archival-quality» materials—to safeguard the city’s documentary heritage, following the conservation guidelines established for the entire country by the Archivo General de la Nación. When you order polyester sleeves for your banknotes, you will be using the same technology Bogotá uses to preserve its colonial documents.
El mundo del coleccionismo privado cuent: The world of private collecting tells the same story. Copies of *Action Comics #1*—Superman’s first appearance, the world’s most valuable comic book, with sales reaching millions of dollars—are preserved and traded in Mylar sleeves; no serious comic collector would use anything else. Major dealers in classic stamps ship their rare pieces in polyester protectors. And the sealed holders used by banknote grading companies such as **PMG** enclose each piece in precisely this kind of inert film: when you buy a certified banknote, it already comes housed in the correct material.
El patrón es imposible de ignorar: bibli: The pattern is impossible to ignore: national libraries, state archives, auction houses, and grading companies—institutions responsible for paper worth fortunes and irreplaceable historical memory—all converged on the same material. No one stores a Magna Carta in PVC.
## Cómo montar un sistema de guarda corr: ## How to set up a proper storage system
Con el diagnóstico claro, el tratamiento: With the diagnosis clear, the treatment is simple and within reach of any budget. A sensible conservation system has three layers:
1. **Primera capa: la funda individual.*: 1. **First layer: the individual sleeve.** Place each banknote in its own appropriately sized archival polyester (Mylar/Melinex) sleeve or, at minimum, an additive-free polypropylene sleeve—the sleeve should extend a few millimeters beyond the banknote on every side, without squeezing it or allowing it to slide around. Manufacturers specializing in archival materials explicitly identify the material and the «acid-free» and «PVC-free» status; that transparency in the technical specifications is itself a sign of quality. Rigid, double-layer polyester holders are available for high-value pieces, as is professional encapsulation by grading companies, which uses precisely this type of sealed inert film. 2. **Second layer: organization.** Individual sleeves go into acid-free cardboard boxes with an alkaline reserve, or into albums whose pages are also made of archival material. Beware of the classic mistake: buying excellent sleeves and placing them in an album with PVC pages. Acidic gases from the album can still reach the banknotes. The conservation chain is only as strong as its weakest link. 3. **Third layer: the environment.** Even the best sleeve cannot compensate for poor surroundings. The ideal conditions are well known: a cool and—more important than the exact value—stable temperature, moderate relative humidity of around 45–55 %, with no sudden fluctuations, and darkness or minimal light, always away from direct sunlight and nearby fluorescent lights. In humid climates, small packets of silica gel (renewed periodically) inside the storage box help enormously, as does choosing an interior cabinet rather than an exterior wall, and never a basement or attic. And one final habit costs nothing: handle banknotes by their edges, with clean, dry hands, over a clear surface.
## No solo billetes: todo el papel colec: ## Not just banknotes: all collectible paper is at stake
Todo lo dicho hasta aquí aplica, casi pa: Almost everything said so far applies word for word to the other paper items we tend to collect alongside banknotes. People who collect paper money also often accumulate stamps, old bank documents, checks, stocks and bonds, postcards, photographs, vintage newspaper clippings, and even tickets and lottery tickets. Each of these objects is cellulose plus ink, and each suffers in PVC exactly as a banknote does: yellowing, bleeding inks, and adhesion to the sleeve.
Algunos merecen advertencias particulare: Some deserve particular warnings. **Stamps** are especially vulnerable because their original gum—the adhesive coating on the back that carries so much weight in their valuation—reacts with moisture and plasticizers with alarming ease: a mint stamp can become fused to a PVC sleeve in just a few years in a humid climate. **Old photographs** add layers of chemical emulsion that PVC gases attack directly; for them, archival polyester is not a recommendation but a requirement of photographic conservation standards. Documents from the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries present the opposite problem: many were printed on inherently acidic wood-pulp paper, so in addition to an inert sleeve, they benefit from enclosures with an alkaline reserve that buffers their own internal deterioration.
Los coleccionistas de historia bancaria: Collectors of banking history—checks from defunct banks, bills of exchange, stock certificates with engraved vignettes—handle pieces that are often unique: there is no other example waiting at the next auction. In those cases, the economic argument falls short; irreplaceable historical documentation is at stake. The good news is that the solution is the same and can be bought in the same place: properly sized polyester sleeves, acid-free boxes, and a stable environment. A single well-designed storage system protects the entire collection, no matter how many types of paper it contains.
## El argumento económico, por si la quí: ## The economic argument, in case the chemistry is not enough
Si todo lo anterior suena abstracto, el: If everything above sounds abstract, the market translates it into numbers with brutal clarity. The price difference between a pristine uncirculated banknote and the same banknote with yellowing, altered color, or plastic residue can be several times its value—and for scarce pieces, the numbers can be painful. Grading companies note conservation problems without mercy, and terms such as «toning» or «residue» on a grading label drive serious buyers away. PVC damage is not an aesthetic imperfection: it is a permanent sentence in the piece’s description, auction after auction.
Hagamos la cuenta contraria: proteger co: Consider the opposite calculation: properly protecting one hundred banknotes with archival polyester sleeves costs less than a single Colombian banknote of moderate interest at an international auction. No other decision in this hobby allows so little money to protect so much value.

1. **Auditoría.** Revisa en qué está gua: 1. **Audit.** Review how your collection is stored. Smell the sleeves, assess their flexibility, and look for yellowing or sticky surfaces. Thirty minutes a year is enough to detect any problem in time.
## La funda como acto de responsabilidad: ## The sleeve as an act of responsibility
Coleccionar billetes es, en el fondo, un: At its heart, collecting banknotes is an exercise in stewardship. The pieces we preserve existed before us and—if we do our job well—will exist after us. Every banknote from Colombia’s nineteenth-century free-banking era, every provisional issue, and every Banco de la República series that survives in collectible condition does so because a chain of people, across generations, chose to care for it.
Elegir Mylar en lugar de PVC no es una s: Choosing Mylar instead of PVC is not the affectation of an obsessive collector: it is our link in that chain. PVC is cheap today and enormously expensive tomorrow; archival polyester costs a few pesos more today and never costs anything again. Rarely does such a small decision so clearly separate preservation from destruction.
Your banknotes cannot choose their sleeve. You can.

Los números más bajos —**00000001, 00000: The lowest numbers—**00000001, 00000002, 00000003**…—are the first printed in an issue and are highly valued because of their rarity and symbolism. The lower the number, the greater the interest.
Todos los dígitos iguales: **7777777**,: All digits are the same: **7777777**, **5555555**. They are extremely scarce and visually striking, hence their high demand.
El número se lee igual de izquierda a de: The number reads the same from left to right and in reverse, such as **1234321** or **4567654**. They are called *radar* or *palindrome* numbers and are a classic of serial-number collecting.
Dígitos en secuencia ascendente o descen: Digits in ascending or descending sequence: **1234567** or **7654321**. They are visually striking and difficult to find without wear.
Patrones como **123123123**, parejas rep: Patterns such as **123123123**, repeated pairs, or recognizable dates also attract interest. Some countries also have **replacement banknotes** (with a star or special mark in the serial number), printed to replace defective pieces and therefore scarcer.
Un número de serie extraordinario dispar: An extraordinary serial number sends the value soaring, but condition remains decisive: a spectacular serial on a heavily circulated banknote is worth far less than on an uncirculated one. Durante buena parte del siglo XIX, Colom: For much of the nineteenth century, Colombia had neither a central bank nor a single currency issued by the state. Instead, a little-known but fascinating system for collectors operated: **free banking**, an era when private banks printed and circulated their own banknotes.
El punto de partida fue la Constitución: The starting point was the Constitution of Rionegro of 1863, which created the **Estados Unidos de Colombia**, a distinctly liberal federal republic. Under its philosophy of minimal economic intervention, founding a bank and issuing banknotes was, in practice, a private activity open to individuals who could raise the necessary capital. There was no state monopoly on issuance.
El **Banco de Bogotá**, fundado en 1870,: The **Banco de Bogotá**, founded in 1870, is often identified as the country’s first modern commercial bank and paved the way for an entire generation of institutions. In the following years, banks emerged in the main commercial centers—Bogotá, Medellín, Barranquilla, Cartagena, and others—each authorized to issue its own banknotes, backed by and redeemable for gold or silver at the bearer’s request.
Cada banco diseñaba e imprimía sus bille: Each bank designed and printed its banknotes, often commissioning the engraving from lithographic firms in Europe or the United States. The result was an enormous variety of designs, denominations, signatures, and vignettes: portraits of national heroes, allegories, and commercial scenes. This diversity, combined with limited print runs and the fragility of period paper, explains why free-banking issues are so sought after by paper money collectors today.
El sistema empezó a cerrarse con la crea: The system began to close with the creation of the **Banco Nacional** in 1880, during the political rise of Rafael Núñez. With the **Regeneration** and the centralist Constitution of 1886, the state took control of issuance: Banco Nacional banknotes were made legal tender, and private banks’ authority to issue currency was progressively restricted. By 1886, the era of free banking had come to an end.

A good example is the [Banco de Medellín 50 centavos banknote](/coleccion/colombia/banco-de-medellin-50-centavos/), a private issue characteristic of the era. At Notofilia, you can explore more examples in our [catalog of Colombian free-banking banknotes](/coleccion/colombia/banca-libre/), featuring issues from various regional banks and their characteristic nineteenth-century designs.

La historia de la banca en Puerto Rico e: The history of banking in Puerto Rico is marked by its dual colonial heritage: first Spanish and, since 1898, American. That transition was recorded on its banknotes and coins, making the island an especially rich field for notaphily.
## El Puerto Rico español y su moneda: ## Spanish Puerto Rico and its currency
Hasta finales del siglo XIX, Puerto Rico: Until the late 19th century, Puerto Rico was an overseas province of Spain. For generations, a diverse mix of metal currency circulated on the island: Spanish colonial pieces, worn cob coins, and foreign coins brought in through trade. The scarcity of a stable and reliable medium of exchange was a recurring problem for the island's economy and laid the groundwork for a formal banking institution.
El **Banco Español de Puerto Rico**, est: The **Banco Español de Puerto Rico**, established in 1888 by royal decree, is generally considered the island's first issuing institution. In addition to the usual functions of a commercial bank—deposits, loans, and discounting—it was granted the authority to issue banknotes denominated in **pesos**, finally giving Puerto Rico its own organized paper currency.
En paralelo, hacia 1895 se acuñó una mon: At the same time, around 1895, a provincial currency specific to the island, the **Puerto Rican peso**, was minted along with its silver fractional denominations. Banco Español banknotes and these provincial coins formed a monetary system distinct from that of mainland Spain, designed to meet the needs of local trade.
## 1898: del peso al dólar: ## 1898: from the peso to the dollar
La Guerra Hispano-Estadounidense y el Tr: The Spanish-American War and the Treaty of Paris of 1898 placed Puerto Rico under United States sovereignty. One of the most immediate and sensitive consequences was monetary: the Puerto Rican peso was withdrawn and replaced by the **U.S. dollar**, at an unfavorable exchange rate that resulted in a loss of value for many island residents.
## Del Banco Español al Banco de Puerto: ## From Banco Español to Banco de Puerto Rico
La propia institución fundacional reflej: The founding institution itself reflected the changing times: Banco Español de Puerto Rico was renamed **Banco de Puerto Rico** in 1913, by then fully integrated into the dollar system. Its issues from the final decades of the 19th century and the beginning of the 20th are now among the most prized pieces in Caribbean notaphily.
Los billetes y monedas de este periodo s: The banknotes and coins from this period are tangible evidence of Puerto Rico's transition from a Spanish colony to a U.S. territory. An emblematic example is the [1895 1-peso exchange note](/coleccion/puerto-rico/billete-de-canje-1-peso-1895/), issued by the Ministry of Overseas Territories in the final years of Spanish sovereignty. You can explore more examples in our [catalog of Puerto Rico banknotes](/coleccion/puerto-rico/).

Si usted colecciona billetes colombianos: If you collect Colombian banknotes, you have surely noticed it: between 1983 and 2014, Banco de la República notes bear three different printer's imprints. Some read **«Imprenta de Billetes – Bogotá»**, others **«Imprenta de Billetes – Santa Fe de Bogotá»**, and the most recent simply **«Banco de la República»**. The Pick catalog even lists them under different abbreviations: IBB and IBSFB. The question naturally arises: are these two or three different companies?
La respuesta es que se trata de **una so: The answer is that they are **one and the same printing works**, and the explanation is a little gem of Colombian history hidden in its paper currency.
## Una imprenta que no es una empresa: ## A printing works that is not a company
La Imprenta de Billetes no es una compañ: The Imprenta de Billetes is not a private company hired by the central bank: it is an **internal division of Banco de la República itself**. It formally began operations on October 23, 1959, with its first job being the 1-peso note designed by Italian Mario Baiardi. It has operated continuously ever since, first in Bogotá's industrial district and later in the complex now known as the Central de Efectivo. In 1994, a Bank of England report praised its technical standards, comparing them with those of European security printers.
## La ciudad que cambió de nombre (dos v: ## The city that changed its name (twice)
Entonces, ¿por qué cambió el pie de impr: So why did the printer's imprint change? The key lies not in the printing works, but in the city where it operates.
La Constitución de 1991 rebautizó oficia: The 1991 Constitution officially renamed the country's capital **«Santa Fe de Bogotá»**. True to official form, the printing works updated its imprint: that is why banknotes from the 1990s bear «Imprenta de Billetes – Santa Fe de Bogotá». It is the same reason why those born in the capital between 1991 and 2000 are, technically, Santafereños rather than Bogotanos.
Un ejemplo que permite estudiar de cerca: One example that offers a close look at this period is the [Banco de la República 2,000 pesos oro note](/coleccion/colombia/banco-de-la-republica-2000-pesos-oro/), listed in the Notofilia catalog with different dates and printers.
En el año 2000, el Acto Legislativo 01 d: In 2000, Legislative Act 01 restored the city's traditional name: **Bogotá D. C.** But instead of reverting the imprint, banknotes began to identify only the issuing and printing institution: «Banco de la República». A change of style, not of printer.

El dato hace aún más valiosa la historia: This fact makes the story of the printing works even more significant. 1. Un Billete Abstracto en un Diner de C: 1. An Abstract Bill in a Chicago Diner
Boggs comenzó a dibujar dinero como obra: Boggs began drawing money as art in 1984, when a Chicago waitress accepted a “very abstract” drawing of a one-dollar bill as payment for a 90-cent check. When she handed back a dime in change, Boggs felt “electricity” in the exchange —the moment that led him to repeat the operation again and again with his own original art.
Sus dibujos, que reproducían solo una ca: His drawings, which reproduced only one face of the note, came to be known as “Boggs bills.” Boggs exchanged them only at face value: when he spent a $100 drawing, he traded it for goods worth exactly that amount.
Cada transacción era en sí misma parte d: Each transaction was itself part of the piece. Boggs later sold the change he received, the purchase receipt, and sometimes the goods themselves, usually to dealers and art collectors —but he never sold the drawn bills directly. Instead he told the collector where and how he had spent each piece, and the buyer had to find the person who held it.
Boggs señalaba que, tras esa transacción: Boggs noted that after that first transaction his bills were often resold for far more than their original face value; the resale of a single “Boggs bill” has been reported at $420,000.
Entre sus obras más conocidas figura una: Among his best-known works is a series of notes made for the annual Florida United Numismatists (“FUN”) convention. Denominations from $1 to $50 borrowed the reverse designs of contemporary U.S. paper money, slightly altered: the legend “THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA” became “FLORIDA UNITED NUMISMATISTS,” and the denomination was occasionally replaced by the acronym “FUN.”
También alteraba detalles visuales &mdas: He also altered visual details —the reflection of Monticello on the $2 note, the Supreme Court building in place of the Treasury on the $10, a different angle of the White House on the $20—. These notes were printed in bright orange on one side and carried Boggs’s autograph and fingerprint on the other.
